what: Nasdaq runs the stock exchange of the same name, but most of its growth now comes from selling software: market surveillance, financial crime detection, risk management for banks, and index licensing.
customers: Listed companies, brokers and traders, banks and asset managers buying software and data, and fund managers licensing indices.
money: trading and clearing fees on equities, options and other markets
listings, index licensing, data and investor relations tools
anti-financial-crime, regulatory and risk software for banks
moat: The exchange has network effects in listings and liquidity, while the software is embedded in bank compliance processes that regulators audit.
risks: Debt of about $9 billion from the Adenza acquisition
Trading volumes fall in calm markets
Listings revenue depends on how many companies go public
Software competes against many well-funded vendors
opportunities: Software and data now provide most revenue and are subscription-based
Index licensing grows with money invested in index funds
A pickup in public listings would lift the exchange business
watch: Annualised recurring revenue in Financial Technology and the number of new listings.
